455:         self._run(["document", "new", "-o", proj_path, "--type", "writer"])
456:         self._run(["--project", proj_path, "writer", "add-heading", "-t", "Title"])
457:         self._run(["--project", proj_path, "export", "render", pdf_path, "-p", "pdf", "--overwrite"])
458:         assert os.path.exists(pdf_path)
459:         with open(pdf_path, "rb") as f:
460:             assert f.read(5) == b"%PDF-"
461: ```
462: 
463:    Run tests in force-installed mode to guarantee the real command is used:
464:    ```bash
465:    CLI_ANYTHING_FORCE_INSTALLED=1 python3 -m pytest cli_anything/<software>/tests/ -v -s
466:    ```
467:    The `-s` flag shows the `[_resolve_cli]` print output confirming which backend
468:    is being used and **prints artifact paths** for manual inspection.
469: 
470: Real-world workflow test scenarios should include:
471: - Multi-segment editing (YouTube-style cut/trim)
472: - Montage assembly (many short clips)
473: - Picture-in-picture compositing
474: - Color grading pipelines
475: - Audio mixing (podcast-style)
476: - Heavy undo/redo stress testing
477: - Save/load round-trips of complex projects
478: - Iterative refinement (add, modify, remove, re-add)
479: 
480: ## Principles & Rules
481: 
482: These are non-negotiable. Every harness MUST follow all of them.
483: 
484: **Backend & Rendering:**
485: - **The real software is a hard dependency.** The CLI MUST invoke the actual application
486:   (LibreOffice, Blender, GIMP, etc.) for rendering and export. Do NOT reimplement
487:   rendering in Python. Do NOT gracefully degrade to a fallback library. If the software
488:   is not installed, error with clear install instructions.
489: - **Manipulate the native format directly** — Parse and modify the app's native project
490:   files (MLT XML, ODF, SVG, etc.) as the data layer.
491: - **Leverage existing CLI tools** — Use `libreoffice --headless`, `blender --background`,
492:   `melt`, `ffmpeg`, `inkscape --actions`, `sox` as subprocesses for rendering.
493: - **Verify rendering produces correct output** — See "The Rendering Gap" in
494:   Architecture Patterns & Pitfalls above.
495: - **Every filter/effect in the registry MUST have a corresponding render mapping**
496:   or be explicitly documented as "project-only (not rendered)".
497: 
498: **CLI Design:**
499: - **Fail loudly and clearly** — Agents need unambiguous error messages to self-correct.
500: - **Be idempotent where possible** — Running the same command twice should be safe.
501: - **Provide introspection** — `info`, `list`, `status` commands are critical for agents
502:   to understand current state before acting.
503: - **Preview meaningful intermediate state** — Harnesses that can expose useful
504:   visual checkpoints SHOULD implement a `preview` command group with at least
505:   `preview recipes`, `preview capture`, and `preview latest`. Diff-oriented
506:   tools SHOULD also expose `preview diff`.
507: - **Keep producer and viewer roles separate** — Harnesses publish preview state
508:   through `cli-anything-<software> preview ...`. `cli-hub previews ...` is the
509:   read-only consumer for inspect/html/watch/open and should not be treated as a
510:   render path.
511: - **Use the shared preview bundle protocol** — Preview-capable harnesses SHOULD
512:   emit `preview-bundle/v1` bundles as described in `docs/PREVIEW_PROTOCOL.md`.
513:   The bundle is the contract; the renderer remains the real software.
514: - **Live preview should separate head vs history** — When a harness supports
515:   `preview live ...`, it SHOULD persist:
516:   - `session.json` as the mutable current head
517:   - immutable bundle directories for each capture
518:   - `trajectory.json` as the append-only command-to-preview history
519: - **Do not treat `_bundle_dir` as the permanent build identity** — It is only a
520:   single snapshot path. Stable live replay should anchor on `session_dir` plus
521:   `trajectory.json`.
522: - **Make `preview live status --json` agent-cheap** — Live-preview harnesses
523:   SHOULD include a compact `trajectory_summary` in `preview live status --json`
524:   so agents do not need to read `trajectory.json` just to understand the latest
525:   command-to-bundle mapping.
526: - **Do not screen-scrape GUI windows for previews** — Preview artifacts must be
527:   produced by the real backend or by native inspection/export paths operating
528:   on real project/capture state.
529: - **JSON output mode** — Every command MUST support `--json` for machine parsing.
530: - **Use the unified REPL skin** — Copy `cli-anything-plugin/repl_skin.py` to
531:   `utils/repl_skin.py` and use `ReplSkin` for banner, prompt, help, and messages.
532:   REPL MUST be the default behavior (`invoke_without_command=True`).
533: 
534: **Testing:**
535: - **E2E tests MUST invoke the real software** and produce real output files (PDF, DOCX,
536:   rendered images, videos). Verify output exists, has correct format (magic bytes, ZIP
537:   structure), and print artifact paths for manual inspection. Never test only
538:   intermediate files.
539: - **Every export/render function MUST be verified** with programmatic output analysis.
540:   "It ran without errors" is not sufficient.
541: - **E2E tests MUST include subprocess tests** that invoke the installed
542:   `cli-anything-<software>` command via `_resolve_cli()`. Tests must work against
543:   the actual installed package, not just source imports.
544: - **Test suites MUST include real-file E2E tests**, not just unit tests with synthetic
545:   data. Format assumptions break constantly with real media.
546: 
547: **Documentation:**
548: - **Every `cli_anything/<software>/` directory MUST contain a `README.md`** explaining
549:   how to install the software dependency, install the CLI, run tests, and basic usage.
550: - **Every `cli_anything/<software>/tests/` directory MUST contain a `TEST.md`**
551:   documenting test coverage, realistic workflows tested, and full test results output.
552: 
553: ### Preview & Live Preview Norms
554: 
555: Preview support is optional at the harness level, but once a harness exposes
556: meaningful intermediate visual or inspection state it MUST follow a consistent
557: contract so agents and humans can reason about it across software.
558: 
559: See [`guides/preview-methodology.md`](guides/preview-methodology.md) for the
560: detailed design guide and documentation checklist.
561: 
562: #### Producer vs consumer roles
563: 
564: Keep these roles separate:
565: 
566: - **Producer** — `cli-anything-<software> preview ...`
567:   - talks to the real backend
568:   - owns preview recipes, source fingerprinting, and live-session publishing
569:   - creates bundles, sessions, and trajectories
570: - **Consumer** — `cli-hub previews ...`
571:   - reads already-published preview state
572:   - provides `inspect`, `html`, `watch`, and `open`
573:   - never renders, replays, or synthesizes preview artifacts
574: 
575: Harness help text, README examples, and SKILL examples MUST not present
576: `cli-hub previews ...` as a render path. Agents should think in two steps:
577: publish with the software CLI, inspect with `cli-hub`.
578: 
579: #### Three-layer persistence model
580: 
581: Preview-capable harnesses SHOULD treat preview state as three separate objects:
582: 
583: - **`bundle_dir`** — an immutable preview snapshot implementing
584:   `preview-bundle/v1`
585: - **`session.json`** — the mutable current head for a live preview stream
586: - **`trajectory.json`** — the append-only permanent command-to-preview history
587: 
588: Do not use `_bundle_dir` as the long-lived identity of a project. It is a
589: single snapshot path and may change whenever the source fingerprint changes or a
590: new bundle is forced. Stable live replay should anchor on `session_dir` plus
591: `trajectory.json`.
592: 
593: #### Recommended CLI surface
594: 
595: If a harness has meaningful previewable state, it SHOULD expose at least:
596: 
597: - `preview recipes`
598: - `preview capture`
599: - `preview latest`
600: 
601: Add the following when the software semantics justify them:
602: 
603: - `preview diff`
604: - `preview live start`
605: - `preview live push`
606: - `preview live status`
607: - `preview live stop`
608: - an internal or hidden poll monitor when poll-first refresh is supported
609: 
610: Recommended semantics:
611: 
612: - `preview capture` renders or exports a fresh bundle unless cache reuse is valid
613: - `preview latest` returns the newest existing bundle and does not render a new one
614: - `preview diff` publishes an immutable comparison bundle
615: - `preview live start` creates a live session and publishes an initial bundle
616: - `preview live push` adds a new bundle to an existing live session
617: - `preview live status` is a read-only status probe
618: - `preview live stop` stops further publishing without deleting prior history
619: 
620: #### Agent-facing JSON contract
621: 
622: All preview commands MUST support `--json`.
623: 
624: At minimum, machine-readable preview results SHOULD expose:
625: 
626: - stable paths such as `_bundle_dir`, `_manifest_path`, and `summary_path`
627: - artifact metadata and relative artifact paths
628: - session metadata when live mode is involved
629: - trajectory references when history exists
630: 
631: `preview live status --json` is especially important because agents call it as a
632: cheap introspection step between mutations. It SHOULD return:
633: 
634: - whether a live session exists and whether it is active
635: - `session_dir`, `session_path`, and current bundle identifiers or paths
636: - current publish reason and latest command metadata when available
637: - a compact `trajectory_summary` with the latest command-to-bundle mapping
638: - viewer hints such as inspect/html/watch/open commands when the harness emits them
639: 
640: The goal is to let an agent understand current live state without rereading the
641: entire `trajectory.json` file.
642: 
643: #### Documentation requirements for preview-capable harnesses
644: 
645: Preview-capable harnesses SHOULD document preview usage in both `README.md` and
646: `SKILL.md`. Cover:
647: 
648: - whether preview support exists at all
649: - which modes exist: static, diff, live, poll
650: - the producer commands agents should call
651: - the consumer commands humans should call with `cli-hub previews ...`
652: - whether the output is images, video, audio-derived stills, inspection JSON, or mixed artifacts
653: - what makes the preview truthful for this software
654: 
655: Use concrete examples that show both the publish step and the inspect/watch
656: step.
657: 
658: #### Truthfulness principle
659: 
660: Preview artifacts MUST be honest views of the real project or capture state.
661: 
662: - Prefer real backend render/export/inspection paths.
663: - Use native offscreen export or replay when the software provides it.
664: - Do not fake renders in Python.
665: - Do not screen-scrape GUI windows just to create something image-like.
666: - If a temporary camera, light, or helper rig must be injected, mark the bundle
667:   status accordingly and explain the limitation in summary/context output.
668: 
669: Truthful previews matter more than pretty previews. Agents need intermediate
670: state they can trust when deciding what to do next.
671: 
672: ## Directory Structure
673: 
674: ```
675: <software>/
676: └── agent-harness/
677:     ├── <SOFTWARE>.md          # Project-specific analysis and SOP
678:     ├── setup.py               # PyPI package configuration (Phase 7)
679:     ├── cli_anything/          # Namespace package (NO __init__.py here)
680:     │   └── <software>/        # Sub-package for this CLI
681:     │       ├── __init__.py
682:     │       ├── __main__.py    # python3 -m cli_anything.<software>
683:     │       ├── README.md      # HOW TO RUN — required
684:     │       ├── <software>_cli.py  # Main CLI entry point (Click + REPL)
685:     │       ├── core/          # Core modules (one per domain)
686:     │       │   ├── __init__.py
687:     │       │   ├── project.py     # Project create/open/save/info
688:     │       │   ├── ...            # Domain-specific modules
689:     │       │   ├── export.py      # Render pipeline + filter translation
690:     │       │   └── session.py     # Stateful session, undo/redo
691:     │       ├── utils/         # Shared utilities
692:     │       │   ├── __init__.py
693:     │       │   ├── <software>_backend.py  # Backend: invokes the real software
694:     │       │   └── repl_skin.py  # Unified REPL skin (copy from plugin)
695:     │       └── tests/         # Test suites
696:     │           ├── TEST.md        # Test documentation and results — required
697:     │           ├── test_core.py   # Unit tests (synthetic data)
698:     │           └── test_full_e2e.py # E2E tests (real files)
699:     └── examples/              # Example scripts and workflows
700: ```
701: 
702: **Critical:** The `cli_anything/` directory must NOT contain an `__init__.py`.
703: This is what makes it a PEP 420 namespace package — multiple separately-installed
704: PyPI packages can each contribute a sub-package under `cli_anything/` without
705: conflicting. For example, `cli-anything-gimp` adds `cli_anything/gimp/` and
706: `cli-anything-blender` adds `cli_anything/blender/`, and both coexist in the
707: same Python environment.
708: 
709: Note: This HARNESS.md is part of the cli-anything-plugin. Individual software directories reference this file — do NOT duplicate it.
710: 
711: ## Applying This to Other Software
712: 
713: This same SOP applies to any GUI application:
714: 
715: | Software | Backend CLI | Native Format | System Package | How the CLI Uses It |
716: |----------|-------------|---------------|----------------|-------------------|
717: | LibreOffice | `libreoffice --headless` | .odt/.ods/.odp (ODF ZIP) | `apt install libreoffice` | Generate ODF → convert to PDF/DOCX/XLSX/PPTX |
718: | Blender | `blender --background --python` | .blend-cli.json | `apt install blender` | Generate bpy script → Blender renders to PNG/MP4 |
719: | GIMP | `gimp -i -b '(script-fu ...)'` | .xcf | `apt install gimp` | Script-Fu commands → GIMP processes & exports |
720: | Inkscape | `inkscape --actions="..."` | .svg (XML) | `apt install inkscape` | Manipulate SVG → Inkscape exports to PNG/PDF |
721: | Shotcut/Kdenlive | `melt` or `ffmpeg` | .mlt (XML) | `apt install melt ffmpeg` | Build MLT XML → melt/ffmpeg renders video |
722: | Audacity | `sox` | .aup3 | `apt install sox` | Generate sox commands → sox processes audio |
723: | OBS Studio | `obs-websocket` | scene.json | `apt install obs-studio` | WebSocket API → OBS captures/records |
724: | Browser (DOMShell) | `npx @apireno/domshell` (MCP) | Accessibility Tree (virtual FS) | `npm install -g npx` (if needed) + Chrome ext | MCP SDK → DOMShell tools → filesystem navigation |
725: 
726: **The software is a required dependency, not optional.** The CLI generates valid
727: intermediate files (ODF, MLT XML, bpy scripts, SVG) and hands them to the real
728: software for rendering. This is what makes the CLI actually useful — it's a
729: command-line interface TO the software, not a replacement for it.
730: 
731: The pattern is always the same: **build the data → call the real software → verify
732: the output**.
733: 
734: ## Guides Reference
735: 
736: Detailed guides live in `guides/`. Use this table to decide which ones to read
737: based on the software you're building a harness for.
738: 
739: | Guide | Read when... | Phase |
740: |-------|-------------|-------|
741: | [`session-locking.md`](guides/session-locking.md) | Implementing session save (all harnesses) | Phase 3 |
742: | [`preview-methodology.md`](guides/preview-methodology.md) | Designing preview, live preview, and agent-facing preview flows | Phase 3, 6.5 |
743: | [`skill-generation.md`](guides/skill-generation.md) | Generating the SKILL.md file | Phase 6.5 |
744: | [`pypi-publishing.md`](guides/pypi-publishing.md) | Packaging and installing the CLI | Phase 7 |
745: | [`mcp-backend.md`](guides/mcp-backend.md) | Software has an MCP server, no native CLI | Phase 3 |
746: | [`filter-translation.md`](guides/filter-translation.md) | Video/audio CLI with effects that need render-time translation | Phase 3 |
747: | [`timecode-precision.md`](guides/timecode-precision.md) | Video/audio CLI with non-integer frame rates (29.97fps, etc.) | Phase 3, 5 |

1: # Auto-Save + --dry-run for One-Shot Commands
2: 
3: Session-based CLIs must auto-save after one-shot mutations and support `--dry-run` to suppress it.
4: 
5: ## Problem
6: 
7: One-shot commands like `cli-anything-kdenlive --project p.json bin import video.mp4` mutate the in-memory project but never call `save_session()`. The project file on disk is unchanged when the process exits — changes are silently lost.
8: 
9: ## Solution
10: 
11: Two additions to `<software>_cli.py`:
12: 
13: ### 1. Add `--dry-run` to the main CLI group
14: 
15: ```python
16: @click.group(invoke_without_command=True)
17: @click.option("--json", "use_json", is_flag=True, help="Output as JSON")
18: @click.option("--project", "project_path", type=str, default=None,
19:               help="Path to project file")
20: @click.option("--dry-run", "dry_run", is_flag=True, default=False,
21:               help="Run command without saving changes to disk")
22: @click.pass_context
23: def cli(ctx, use_json, project_path, dry_run):
24:     ...
25: ```
26: 
27: ### 2. Add `@cli.result_callback()` after the group
28: 
29: ```python
30: @cli.result_callback()
31: def auto_save_on_exit(result, use_json, project_path, dry_run, **kwargs):
32:     """Auto-save project after one-shot commands if state was modified."""
33:     if _repl_mode:
34:         return
35:     if dry_run:
36:         return
37:     sess = get_session()
38:     if sess.has_project() and sess._modified and sess.project_path:
39:         try:
40:             sess.save_session()
41:         except Exception as e:
42:             click.echo(f"Warning: Auto-save failed: {e}", err=True)
43: ```
44: 
45: **How it works:**
46: - `result_callback` fires once after the CLI group's command chain completes
47: - Checks `_repl_mode` (skip in REPL — user saves manually), `dry_run` (skip if set), and `sess._modified` (skip if nothing changed)
48: - Calls `sess.save_session()` which uses atomic `_locked_save_json` (see [`session-locking.md`](session-locking.md))
49: - Does NOT fire if `sys.exit(1)` was called in `handle_error` (error path) — correct behavior
50: 
51: ### Alternative: `ctx.call_on_close` pattern
52: 
53: For harnesses that open the session inline (not via a global singleton), use a closure instead:
54: 
55: ```python
56: def cli(ctx, use_json, project_path, dry_run):
57:     ...
58:     if project_path:
59:         sess = get_session()
60:         proj = proj_mod.open_project(project_path)
61:         sess.set_project(proj, project_path)
62: 
63:         def _auto_save():
64:             if dry_run:
65:                 return
66:             if sess._modified and sess.project_path and not _repl_mode:
67:                 sess.save_session()
68: 
69:         ctx.call_on_close(_auto_save)
70: ```
71: 
72: ## `--dry-run` semantics
73: 
74: | Mode | Behavior |
75: |------|----------|
76: | One-shot (default) | Command executes, output is printed, project is auto-saved |
77: | One-shot + `--dry-run` | Command executes, output is printed, project is **not** saved |
78: | REPL | `--dry-run` is accepted but ignored (REPL never auto-saves) |
79: 
80: ## When this applies
81: 
82: **Required** for any harness where:
83: - `core/session.py` exists with `save_session()` and `_modified` tracking
84: - The CLI accepts a `--project` flag to load a file-backed project
85: - Commands call `sess.snapshot()` before mutations
86: 
87: **Does not apply** to stateless API clients, service wrappers, or harnesses without a persistent project file.

1: # Session File Locking
2: 
3: When saving session JSON, use exclusive file locking to prevent concurrent writes from corrupting data.
4: 
5: ## The Problem
6: 
7: Never use bare `open("w") + json.dump()` — `open("w")` truncates the file before any lock can be acquired.
8: 
9: ## The Solution: `_locked_save_json`
10: 
11: Open with `"r+"`, lock, then truncate inside the lock:
12: 
13: ```python
14: def _locked_save_json(path, data, **dump_kwargs) -> None:
15:     """Atomically write JSON with exclusive file locking."""
16:     try:
17:         f = open(path, "r+")            # no truncation on open
18:     except FileNotFoundError:
19:         os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path)), exist_ok=True)
20:         f = open(path, "w")             # first save — file doesn't exist yet
21:     with f:
22:         _locked = False
23:         try:
24:             import fcntl
25:             fcntl.flock(f.fileno(), fcntl.LOCK_EX)
26:             _locked = True
27:         except (ImportError, OSError):
28:             pass                        # Windows / unsupported FS — proceed unlocked
29:         try:
30:             f.seek(0)
31:             f.truncate()                # truncate INSIDE the lock
32:             json.dump(data, f, **dump_kwargs)
33:             f.flush()
34:         finally:
35:             if _locked:
36:                 fcntl.flock(f.fileno(), fcntl.LOCK_UN)
37: ```
38: 
39: Copy this pattern into `core/session.py` for all session saves.

1: # PyPI Publishing and Installation (Phase 7)
2: 
3: After building and testing the CLI, make it installable and discoverable.
4: 
5: All cli-anything CLIs use **PEP 420 namespace packages** under the shared
6: `cli_anything` namespace. This allows multiple CLI packages to be installed
7: side-by-side in the same Python environment without conflicts.
8: 
9: ## 1. Package Structure
10: 
11: ```
12: agent-harness/
13: ├── setup.py
14: └── cli_anything/           # NO __init__.py here (namespace package)
15:     └── <software>/         # e.g., gimp, blender, audacity
16:         ├── __init__.py     # HAS __init__.py (regular sub-package)
17:         ├── <software>_cli.py
18:         ├── core/
19:         ├── utils/
20:         └── tests/
21: ```
22: 
23: The key rule: `cli_anything/` has **no** `__init__.py`. Each sub-package
24: (`gimp/`, `blender/`, etc.) **does** have `__init__.py`. This is what
25: enables multiple packages to contribute to the same namespace.
26: 
27: ## 2. setup.py Template
28: 
29: Create `setup.py` in the `agent-harness/` directory:
30: 
31: ```python
32: from setuptools import setup, find_namespace_packages
33: 
34: setup(
35:     name="cli-anything-<software>",
36:     version="1.0.0",
37:     packages=find_namespace_packages(include=["cli_anything.*"]),
38:     install_requires=[
39:         "click>=8.0.0",
40:         "prompt-toolkit>=3.0.0",
41:         # Add Python library dependencies here
42:     ],
43:     entry_points={
44:         "console_scripts": [
45:             "cli-anything-<software>=cli_anything.<software>.<software>_cli:main",
46:         ],
47:     },
48:     python_requires=">=3.10",
49: )
50: ```
51: 
52: **Important details:**
53: - Use `find_namespace_packages`, NOT `find_packages`
54: - Use `include=["cli_anything.*"]` to scope discovery
55: - Entry point format: `cli_anything.<software>.<software>_cli:main`
56: - The **system package** (LibreOffice, Blender, etc.) is a **hard dependency**
57:   that cannot be expressed in `install_requires`. Document it in README.md and
58:   have the backend module raise a clear error with install instructions:
59:   ```python
60:   # In utils/<software>_backend.py
61:   def find_<software>():
62:       path = shutil.which("<software>")
63:       if path:
64:           return path
65:       raise RuntimeError(
66:           "<Software> is not installed. Install it with:\n"
67:           "  apt install <software>   # Debian/Ubuntu\n"
68:           "  brew install <software>  # macOS"
69:       )
70:   ```
71: 
72: ## 3. Import Convention
73: 
74: All imports use the `cli_anything.<software>` prefix:
75: 
76: ```python
77: from cli_anything.gimp.core.project import create_project
78: from cli_anything.gimp.core.session import Session
79: from cli_anything.blender.core.scene import create_scene
80: ```
81: 
82: ## 4. Verification Steps
83: 
84: **Test local installation:**
85: ```bash
86: cd /root/cli-anything/<software>/agent-harness
87: pip install -e .
88: ```
89: 
90: **Verify PATH installation:**

2: 
3: Generate a SKILL.md file that makes the CLI discoverable and usable by AI agents
4: through the skill-creator methodology. This file serves as a self-contained skill
5: definition that can be loaded by Claude Code or other AI assistants.
6: 
7: ## Purpose
8: 
9: SKILL.md files follow a standard format that enables AI agents to:
10: - Discover the CLI's capabilities
11: - Understand command structure and usage
12: - Generate correct command invocations
13: - Handle output programmatically
14: 
15: ## SKILL.md Structure
16: 
17: ### 1. YAML Frontmatter — Triggering metadata for skill discovery:
18: 
19: ```yaml
20: ---
21: name: "cli-anything-<software>"
22: description: "Brief description of what the CLI does"
23: ---
24: ```
25: 
26: ### 2. Markdown Body — Usage instructions including:
27: 
28: - Installation prerequisites
29: - Basic command syntax
30: - Command groups and their functions
31: - Usage examples
32: - Agent-specific guidance (JSON output, error handling)
33: 
34: ## Generation Process
35: 
36: ### 1. Extract CLI metadata using `skill_generator.py`:
37: 
38: ```python
39: from skill_generator import generate_skill_file
40: 
41: skill_path = generate_skill_file(
42:     harness_path="/path/to/agent-harness"
43: )
44: # Default output: skills/cli-anything-<software>/SKILL.md
45: ```
46: 
47: ### 2. The generator automatically extracts:
48: 
49: - Software name and version from setup.py
50: - Command groups from the CLI file (Click decorators)
51: - Documentation from README.md
52: - System package requirements
53: 
54: ### 3. Customize the template (optional):
55: 
56: - Default template: `templates/SKILL.md.template`
57: - Uses Jinja2 placeholders for dynamic content
58: - Can be extended for software-specific sections
59: 
60: ## Output Location
61: 
62: SKILL.md is generated canonically at the repo root, with a packaged compatibility
63: copy for installed harnesses:
64: 
65: ```
66: skills/
67: └── cli-anything-<software>/
68:     └── SKILL.md
69: 
70: <software>/
71: └── agent-harness/
72:     └── cli_anything/
73:         └── <software>/
74:             └── skills/
75:                 └── SKILL.md
76: ```
77: 
78: ## Manual Generation
79: 
80: ```bash
81: cd cli-anything-plugin
82: python skill_generator.py /path/to/software/agent-harness
83: ```

86: 
87: The SKILL.md generation should be run after Phase 6 (Test Documentation) completes
88: successfully, ensuring the CLI is fully documented and tested before creating the
89: skill definition.

94: - Include agent-specific guidance for programmatic usage
95: - Document `--json` flag usage for machine-readable output
96: - List all command groups with brief descriptions
97: - Provide realistic examples that demonstrate common workflows

116: packaged copy, displaying whichever absolute path is available in the startup
117: banner. AI agents can read the file at the displayed path:

25: > dependency manager and use it correctly. Do NOT override the project's

30: > **Reactive Environment Check Bundling (Only When Installing)**: Do NOT run
31: > environment or package availability checks (`importlib.util.find_spec`,
32: > `pip list`, `ls uv.lock...`) proactively before writing code or creating a

39: >   <pkg>` or `%pip list`) and install missing packages (`%pip install`)
40: >   **inside notebook cells**, never via `python3 -c` or `pip` in the shell.
41: > - **In the Shell (Only When Installing)**: When a shell check is required
42: >   before installing a missing package for a local script or project, you MUST
43: >   NOT run multiple sequential 1-line shell check commands. Combine all
44: >   environment and package availability probes into a single composite python
45: >   one-liner or shell check step:
46: >
47: > ```bash
48: > python3 -c "import sys, importlib.util; print(f'Python {sys.version.split()[0]}'); [(print(f'{pkg}: {__import__(pkg).__version__}') if importlib.util.find_spec(pkg) else print(f'{pkg}: not found')) for pkg in ['pyspark', 'google.cloud.bigquery']]"
49: > ```
50: >
51: > This bundling also applies to dependency manager detection; when an install is
52: > needed, use a single `ls` or `find` command to check for all potential
53: > dependency manager configuration and lock files at once (e.g. `ls uv.lock
54: > poetry.lock Pipfile.lock requirements.txt pyproject.toml`).

56: ## Dependency Manager Detection (Only When Installing)
57: 
58: Only run dependency manager detection when a package actually needs to be
59: installed (e.g., on `ModuleNotFoundError` / `ImportError` or when setting up a
60: missing local project environment)—never as an upfront pre-flight check before
61: creating or running a notebook. Before installing ANY Python package, check the
62: workspace for these files **in priority order**:
63: 
64: 1.  **Signal:** `uv.lock` or `pyproject.toml` with `[tool.uv]`
65:     *   **Tool:** **uv**
66:     *   **Install:** `uv add <package>`
67:     *   **Setup:** `uv sync`
68: 2.  **Signal:** `pyproject.toml` with `[tool.poetry]`
69:     *   **Tool:** **Poetry**
70:     *   **Install:** `poetry add <package>`
71:     *   **Setup:** `poetry install`
72: 3.  **Signal:** `Pipfile`

75:     *   **Setup:** `pipenv install`
76: 4.  **Signal:** `environment.yml`
77:     *   **Tool:** **Conda**
78:     *   **Install:** `conda install <package>`
79:     *   **Setup:** `conda env create -f environment.yml`
80: 5.  **Signal:** `requirements.txt` only
81:     *   **Tool:** **venv + pip**
82:     *   **Install:** `.venv/bin/pip install <package>`
83:     *   **Setup:** `.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt`
84: 6.  **Signal:** None of the above
85:     *   **Tool:** **venv + pip** (default)
86:     *   **Install:** `.venv/bin/pip install <package>`
87:     *   **Setup:** `.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt`
88: 
89: ## Default: venv + pip
90: 
91: If no dependency manager is detected, use **venv + pip + requirements.txt** as
92: the default:
93: 
94: ```bash
95: # Initialize environment
96: python3 -m venv .venv
97: 
98: # Add dependencies
99: .venv/bin/pip install <package>
100: 
101: # Preserve state
102: .venv/bin/pip freeze > requirements.txt
103: ```
104: 
105: **Rules for venv + pip workflow:**
106: 
107: -   Always use `.venv/bin/pip` or `.venv/bin/python` (explicit path).
108: -   After installing, run: `.venv/bin/pip freeze > requirements.txt`.
109: -   When setting up: `.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt`.

112: # Quick Start
113: 
114: The `demo.py` example creates a CapCut draft with audio/video media and a line of text, and adds audio fade-in, a video intro animation, a transition, keyframes, and text bubble/fancy text effects.
115: 
116: How to run the example:
117: 
118: 1. Find your CapCut Drafts folder path (like `.../CapCut Drafts`) and replace `<your CapCut Drafts folder>` in the code
119: 2. Run `demo.py` (the example overwrites an existing draft named `demo`; make sure it is safe to replace)
120: 3. In CapCut, find and open the newly created `demo` draft (you may need to enter and exit an existing draft, or restart CapCut to refresh the list). You should see a timeline similar to the image below:
121: 
122: ![Quick Start](readme_assets/快速上手.png)
123: 
124: Adjust the media, timing and effects in the example to create your own draft. Export the finished video manually in CapCut.

126: # Usage Guide
127: 
128: > ℹ It’s recommended to jump to interesting features from the [Feature List](#feature-list) instead of reading sequentially.
129: 
130: ### Template Mode
131: 
132: Templates must contain a readable, plaintext `draft_content.json`. Encrypted or otherwise unreadable formats are not supported.
133: 
134: To retain certain complex features (text effects, compound clips, etc.), you can load an existing CapCut draft as a template, then import parts of it into another draft, or directly replace part of its segments.
135: 
136: Currently three replacement methods are provided:
137: 
138: - [Replace media by name](#replace-media-by-name): replace the media itself, affecting all segments that reference it
139: - [Replace media by segment](#replace-media-by-segment): replace the media of a specific segment and reselect the source range it references
140: - [Replace the content of text segments](#replace-text-segment-content): keep all text formatting while replacing its content
141: 
142: Additionally, for items without a clear name (stickers, fancy text, etc.), [extract resource metadata](#extract-resource-metadata) to obtain their `resource_id`.
143: 
144: > ℹ If you encounter missing template content, please report it.
145: 
146: #### Load Template
147: 
148: It is recommended to use `DraftFolder` to manage CapCut’s drafts folder (found in CapCut “Global Settings” → “Drafts Location”), which makes it convenient to generate a new draft from a template.
149: 
150: ```python
151: import pycapcut as cc
152: 
153: draft_folder = cc.DraftFolder("<CapCut Drafts folder>")  # Usually like ".../CapCut Drafts"
154: script = draft_folder.duplicate_as_template("Template Draft", "New Draft")  # Copy "Template Draft" to a new draft named "New Draft" and return an editable ScriptFile object
155: 
156: # Edit the returned ScriptFile object, e.g., replace media, add tracks and segments
157: script.save()  # Save your "New Draft"
158: ```
159: 
160: To maximize compatibility with complex features in templates, the imported tracks are kept separate from the tracks created by pycapcut:
161: 
162: - Other than the replacement features below, you cannot add segments, transitions, fades, effects, etc. on imported tracks
163: - You can still create new tracks and add segments as in non-template mode
164: 
165: #### Extract Resource Metadata
166: 
167: For an imported `ScriptFile`, call `inspect_material` to extract `resource_id` for certain materials. `DraftFolder` also offers methods to inspect resource metadata of a specified draft.
168: 
169: ```python
170: import pycapcut as cc
171: 
172: draft_folder = cc.DraftFolder("<CapCut Drafts folder>")
173: draft_folder.inspect_material("Draft Name")
174: 
175: # Or
176: script = draft_folder.load_template("Draft Name")
177: script.inspect_material()
178: ```
179: 
180: The output might look like:
181: 
182: ```
183: 贴纸素材:
184:         Resource id: 7405878923323641129 '秋日手绘-枫叶'
185:         Resource id: 7429353555447893260 '电商购物促销/哇哦'
186:         Resource id: 7437707455267671315 '冬日涂鸦winter雪花冬天vlog装饰文字'
187:         Resource id: 7343931192204463401 '爱心'
188: 文字气泡效果:
189:         Effect id: 763870 ,Resource id: 6838834573413978631 '标题59'
190: 花字效果:
191:         Resource id: 7342020000812731658 '彩色手绘线条花字'
192: ```
193: 
194: The metadata above can be used to add corresponding materials (e.g., via the `resource_id` parameter of `StickerSegment`).
195: 
196: #### Replace Media by Name
197: 
198: This approach replaces the media itself without directly modifying segments.
199: 
200: > ℹ Since materials have names (by default, the local file name), this replacement is easy to locate
201: 
202: > ℹ Because it doesn’t involve source range changes, this method is especially suitable for image media and rarely causes compatibility issues
203: 
204: Using the draft from [Quick Start](#quick-start) as an example, if we want to replace the audio media with a new one:
205: ```python
206: new_material = cc.AudioMaterial("<path to new audio file>")
207: script.replace_material_by_name("audio.mp3", new_material)  # Replace the material named "audio.mp3"
208: ```
209: 
210: After replacement, the segment still trims the first 5 seconds of the media, and properties like volume, fade in/out, playback speed remain unchanged.
211: 
212: #### Replace Media by Segment
213: 
214: This approach replaces a specific segment’s media, allowing you to reselect the source range and stretch/shrink the segment on the timeline accordingly.
215: 
216: > ℹ Since segments have no names, you usually need to locate them by index
217: 
218: This involves two steps: select a track and then replace the media. Using the audio example above:
219: ```python
220: from pycapcut import trange_seconds, ShrinkMode, ExtendMode
221: 
222: audio_track = script.get_imported_track(
223:     cc.TrackType.audio,                # Select the imported audio track
224:     #name="audio",                         # If the track has a name, prefer using it
225:     index=0                                # Or locate by index; 0 means the bottom-most track of the same type
226: )
227: 
228: script.replace_material_by_seg(
229:     audio_track, 0, new_material,          # Select the 0-th segment in audio_track (i.e., the first segment)
230:     #source_timerange=None,                # If not specified, default to use the entire material
231:     source_timerange=trange_seconds(0, duration=10),  # Here we select the first 10 seconds of the material (note original segment length is 5s)
232:     handle_shrink=ShrinkMode.cut_tail,     # If the segment shortens, move its end earlier
233:     handle_extend=ExtendMode.push_tail     # If the segment extends, move its end later; push following segments if needed
234: )
235: ```
236: 
237: As seen above, this may change the segment duration, so use `handle_shrink` and `handle_extend` to specify behavior when shortening or extending.
238: 
239: > ℹ Default behavior when not specifying `handle_shrink`/`handle_extend`:
240: > - If the new media is shorter than the original, move the segment end earlier to match the new length
241: > - If the new media is longer than the original, crop the source range to keep the segment duration unchanged
242: 
243: See enum classes `ShrinkMode` and `ExtendMode` for the full list of behaviors.
244: 
245: > ℹ It’s known that replacing segments with combined in/out animations does not automatically refresh animation timing
246: 
247: #### Replace Text Segment Content
248: 
249: This replaces the content of a specific text segment while keeping all formatting.
250: 
251: This also involves two steps: select a track and then replace the content. The “select track” step is similar to [Replace Media by Segment](#replace-media-by-segment).
252: 
253: Assuming we already selected a text track `text_track`:
254: ```python
255: script.replace_text(
256:     text_track, 0,  # Select the 0-th segment in text_track (i.e., the first segment)
257:     "New text content"     # New text content
258: )
259: ```
260: 
261: #### Import Tracks from a Template Draft
262: 
263: This literally copies the specified tracks in the template draft into the new draft. Suitable for stitching multiple templates together.
264: 
265: > ℹ Currently only audio/video/text tracks are supported.
266: 
267: > ⚠️ This method preserves IDs of segments and their materials, therefore you cannot import the same track into the same draft multiple times.
268: 
269: Example:
270: ```python
271: source_script = draft_folder.load_template("<Template Draft Name>")     # Load the template draft
272: target_script = draft_folder.create_draft("New Draft", 1920, 1080)  # Create a new draft
273: 
274: # Select a text track from the template
275: text_track = source_script.get_imported_track(
276:     cc.TrackType.text,                # Select imported text track
277:     #name="text",                        # If the track has a name, prefer using it
278:     index=0                              # Or locate by index; 0 means the bottom-most track of the same type
279: )
280: 
281: # Import the text track into the new draft
282: target_script.import_track(
283:     source_script, text_track,
284:     offset=target_script.duration,  # Place the imported track at the end of the new draft
285:     new_name="imported_text",       # Optional new track name
286:     relative_index=1,               # Relative order among all text tracks; larger values are closer to the foreground; can be negative
287: )
288: ```
289: 
290: ### Time and Tracks
291: 
292: #### Time Format
293: 
294: CapCut (and this project) internally stores time in microseconds, which is not convenient to input. We provide a “string form” for time. Most time parameters support both:
295: 
296: - Microseconds: `int`, suitable for calculation
297: - String: `str`, like `"1.5s"`, `"1h3m12s"`, convenient for input
298: 
299: If you want to explicitly convert from string to microseconds, use `tim`. `trange` is a convenience constructor for `Timerange` that accepts string inputs.
300: 
301: For most uses, prefer `trange_seconds(start, end=...)` or `trange_seconds(start, duration=...)`. All arguments are in seconds; supply exactly one of `end` and `duration`. Start and end are rounded separately to microseconds, then used to calculate the duration. `trange` continues to accept microseconds or time strings.
302: 
303: Rounding can make the same duration differ by one microsecond at different start times. For adjacent segments, use `end` to specify their shared absolute boundary.
304: 
305: > ⚠️ The second parameter of `trange` is the duration, not the end time
306: 
307: For example:
308: ```python
309: import pycapcut as cc
310: from pycapcut import SEC, tim, trange
311: 
312: # 1 second
313: assert 1000000 == SEC == tim("1s") == tim("0.01666667m")
314: 
315: # 0~1 minute
316: assert cc.Timerange(0, 60*SEC) == trange("0s", "1m") == trange("0s", "0.5m30s")
317: 
318: # 2 seconds after a segment starts
319: seg = cc.TextSegment("Example", cc.trange_seconds(0, duration=4))
320: assert seg.target_timerange.start + 2*SEC == seg.target_timerange.start + tim("2s")
321: 
322: # Specify the shared absolute boundary for adjacent segments
323: first = cc.trange_seconds(0, end=1.25)
324: second = cc.trange_seconds(1.25, end=2.5)
325: assert first.end == second.start
326: ```
327: 
328: #### Source Trimming and Global Speed
329: 
330: Trimming and speed are configured when creating a `Segment`, via `target_timerange`, `source_timerange`, and `speed`.
331: > ℹ Curve speed change is not yet supported
332: 
333: Using `VideoSegment` as example (same for `AudioSegment`). Two construction styles are supported:
334: 
335: 1. Convenience constructor: pass a media path string directly to auto-create a material instance
336: 2. Traditional constructor: create the material instance first, then pass it to the segment constructor. Use this when you need to set crop properties on the media.
337: 
338: ```python
339: import os
340: import pycapcut as cc
341: from pycapcut import trange, trange_seconds, SEC
342: 
343: # Assume we already have a draft object `script` (see “Quick Start”), and create three tracks
344: for i in range(3, 0, -1): # reverse order
345:     script.add_track(cc.TrackType.video, "%d" % i)
346: 
347: # The following demonstrates creation of materials and segments
348: # Method 1: convenience constructor (recommended)
349: tutorial_asset_dir = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), 'readme_assets', 'tutorial')
350: video_path = os.path.join(tutorial_asset_dir, 'video.mp4')
351: 
352: # Pass the media path directly
353: seg1 = cc.VideoSegment(video_path, trange_seconds(0, duration=4))  # Trim the first 4 seconds of the material
354: 
355: # Method 2: traditional constructor
356: mat = cc.VideoMaterial(video_path)  # Create the material instance first
357: seg2 = cc.VideoSegment(mat, trange_seconds(0, duration=4))  # Then pass it to the constructor
358: 
359: # The video material length is 5s
360: print("Video material length: %f s" % (mat.duration / SEC))
361: 
362: # The following demonstrates source trimming and speed
363: # If source_timerange is not specified, the first segment of equal length is used automatically
364: seg11 = cc.VideoSegment(video_path, trange_seconds(0, duration=4))              # Automatically trim first 4 seconds (4 seconds is the duration)
365: seg2  = cc.VideoSegment(video_path, trange_seconds(0, duration=4), speed=1.25)  # Automatically trim the first 4*1.25=5 seconds
366: # seg4 = cc.VideoSegment(video_path, trange_seconds(0, duration=3), speed=3.0)   # Trim the first 3*3.0=9 seconds; will error if material is too short
367: # If source_timerange is specified, trim the specified range and auto-set speed
368: seg12 = cc.VideoSegment(video_path, trange_seconds(4, duration=1),
369:                             source_timerange=trange_seconds(0, duration=4))     # Play 4s of material within 1s; speed auto-set to 4.0
370: 
371: # If both source_timerange and speed are specified, trim the specified range and override target duration by speed
372: seg3  = cc.VideoSegment(video_path, trange("1s", "66666h"),
373:                             source_timerange=trange_seconds(0, duration=5),
374:                             speed=2.0) # Play 5s of material at 2x speed; target duration becomes 2.5s
375: 
376: # Add segments to tracks
377: script.add_segment(seg11, "1").add_segment(seg12, "1")
378: script.add_segment(seg2, "2")
379: script.add_segment(seg3, "3")
380: ```
381: 
382: #### Pitch Change During Speed Adjustment
383: 
384: Set `change_pitch=True` on `AudioSegment` or a `VideoSegment` with audio to change pitch along with playback speed. The default is `False`, preserving the original pitch during speed adjustment. A video without audio has no audible change.
385: 
386: ```python
387: audio_path = os.path.join(tutorial_asset_dir, 'audio.mp3')
388: 
389: audio_segment = cc.AudioSegment(audio_path, trange_seconds(0, duration=2),
390:                                 speed=2.0, change_pitch=True)
391: ```
392: 
393: #### Main Track Magnet
394: 
395: Set `maintrack_adsorb` when creating a draft to control the main track magnet. It is enabled by default.
396: 
397: ```python
398: script = draft_folder.create_draft("New Draft", 1920, 1080, maintrack_adsorb=False)
399: script.save()
400: ```
401: 
402: #### Multi-Track Operations
403: 
404: `ScriptFile.add_track` supports creating multiple tracks of the same type and customizing their order:
405: ```python
406: script.add_track(cc.TrackType.video,
407:                  track_name="Foreground",       # Track name
408:                  relative_index=2)              # Relative position among all video tracks
409: script.add_track(cc.TrackType.video,
410:                  track_name="Background",
411:                  relative_index=1)              # Since 1 < 2, the background track is below the foreground
412: ```
413: 
414: > ℹ For tracks with the same index, tracks created later are placed on top by default
415: 
416: Once multiple tracks of the same type exist, you must specify the target track when adding segments, e.g.:
417: ```python
418: script.add_segment(video_segment, "Background")
419: ```
420: 
421: ### Global Video Adjustments
422: 
423: Set rotation, flip, scale, opacity and position through the `clip_settings` parameter of `VideoSegment`. Set media cropping through the `crop_settings` parameter of `VideoMaterial`.
424: > ℹ Keyframes have higher priority than global adjustments, so keyframes override corresponding global settings
425: 
426: Example: create a video segment and set its opacity to 0.5 and enable horizontal flip:
427: ```python
428: from pycapcut import ClipSettings
429: video_segment = cc.VideoSegment(video_material,
430:                                    cc.Timerange(0, video_material.duration),      # Same length as the material
431:                                    clip_settings=ClipSettings(alpha=0.5,             # Opacity 0.5
432:                                                               flip_horizontal=True)  # Enable horizontal flip
433:                                     )
434: ```
435: 
436: See the `ClipSettings` constructor for detailed parameters.
437: 
438: ### Keyframes
439: 
440: A keyframe is a pair of (time within the segment, value) attached to a segment. To create keyframes, call `add_keyframe` with the time relative to the segment start, the value, and the property to control.
441: > ℹ Currently keyframes for effect or filter parameters are not supported
442: 
443: The following example simulates a fade-out using two opacity keyframes:
444: ```python
445: import os
446: import pycapcut as cc
447: from pycapcut import KeyframeProperty, SEC
448: 
449: # Assume we already have a draft object `script` (see “Quick Start”), and create a video track
450: script.add_track(cc.TrackType.video)
451: tutorial_asset_dir = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), 'readme_assets', 'tutorial')
452: 
453: # Create a video segment
454: video_material = cc.VideoMaterial(os.path.join(tutorial_asset_dir, 'video.mp4'))
455: video_segment = cc.VideoSegment(video_material,
456:                                    cc.Timerange(0, video_material.duration)) # Same length as the material
457: 
458: # Add two opacity keyframes to make a 1s fade-out
459: video_segment.add_keyframe(KeyframeProperty.alpha, video_segment.duration - SEC, 1.0) # Fully opaque 1s before end
460: video_segment.add_keyframe(KeyframeProperty.alpha, video_segment.duration, 0.0) # Fully transparent at end
461: 
462: # Add the segment to the track
463: script.add_segment(video_segment)
464: ```
465: 
466: Besides `alpha`, `KeyframeProperty` includes translation, rotation, scale, volume, saturation, etc., all of which support keyframes. Text and sticker segments also support keyframes for position-/size-related properties only.
467: 
468: For audio segments, currently only volume keyframes are supported, and you do not need to specify `KeyframeProperty`:
469: ```python
470: audio_segment: cc.AudioSegment
471: audio_segment.add_keyframe("0s", 0.6) # Volume is 60% at the start of the segment
472: ```
473: 
474: ### Audio Fades
475: 
476: Call `add_fade(in_duration, out_duration)` on an audio segment or a video segment with audio to set its audio fade-in and fade-out durations. Use time strings or microseconds. Each segment can have one fade configuration.
477: 
478: ```python
479: audio_segment.add_fade("1s", "0.5s")
480: video_segment.add_fade("0.5s", "1s")
481: ```
482: 
483: Set volume through the segment constructor’s `volume` parameter; `1.0` keeps the original volume. Use [keyframes](#keyframes) to change volume over time.
484: 
485: ### Masks
486: 
487: Adding masks is simple: call `VideoSegment.add_mask`:
488: ```python
489: from pycapcut import MaskType
490: 
491: # Add a linear mask centered at (100, 0) pixels on the material, rotated 45 degrees clockwise
492: video_segment1.add_mask(MaskType.线性, center_x=100, rotation=45)
493: # Add a circular mask with diameter 50% of the material
494: video_segment2.add_mask(MaskType.圆形, size=0.5)
495: ```
496: Where:
497: 
498: - `MaskType` stores CapCut’s built-in mask types
499: - `center_x` and `center_y` are the mask center coordinates, same meaning as in CapCut
500: - `rotation`, `feather`, and `round_corner` correspond to rotation, feathering, and round-corner parameters, same as in CapCut
501: - `size` is the “primary size” (visible surface height/ circle diameter/ heart height, etc.) as a proportion of the material
502: 
503: See the `add_mask` docstring for more details.
504: 
505: ### Effects, Animations, and Filters
506: 
507: #### Effect Types
508: 
509: Currently supported effect enums:
510: 
511: - Audio: `AudioSceneEffectType` (scene audio), `ToneEffectType` (tone)
512: - Video: `VideoSceneEffectType` (visual effects), `VideoCharacterEffectType` (character effects)
513: 
514: Currently supported animation enums:
515: 
516: - Video: `IntroType` (intro), `OutroType` (outro), `GroupAnimationType` (group animation)
517: - Text: `TextIntro` (intro), `TextOutro` (outro), `TextLoopAnim` (looping animation)
518: 
519: Filter types are in `FilterType`, only for video segments.
520: 
521: Enum members are (usually) named directly after effect/filter names, with parameter annotations, for example:
522: 
523: ![Effect Types](readme_assets/片段特效_annotation.jpg)
524: 
525: You can also use `from_name` to get a specific member, ignoring case, spaces, and underscores, e.g.:
526: 
527: ```python
528: from pycapcut import VideoSceneEffectType
529: 
530: assert VideoSceneEffectType.from_name("__全息 扫描__") == VideoSceneEffectType.全息扫描
531: ```
532: 
533: > ⚠️ Not all enum-listed effects are necessarily usable. Please verify the effect can be found in the CapCut UI before using it.
534: 
535: #### Add Segment Effects
536: 
537: Use `segment.add_effect()` to add effects. It accepts an effect type and a parameter array. The parameter order matches the order in the effect type’s annotations, which may differ from the order in the CapCut UI.
538: 
539: Example: add the `全息扫描` effect to a video segment, set `氛围` to 100 (CapCut value), others default:
540: ```python
541: from pycapcut import VideoSceneEffectType
542: 
543: video_segment.add_effect(VideoSceneEffectType.全息扫描,
544:                          [None, None, 100.0]) # Leave first two params unset; third param (氛围) is 100; others unset
545: ```
546: Audio segment effects are added similarly. For the “花栗鼠” tone, the two parameters are pitch and timbre. Both range from 0 to 100 and default to 50:
547: 
548: ```python
549: from pycapcut import ToneEffectType
550: 
551: audio_segment.add_effect(ToneEffectType.花栗鼠, [50, 42])
552: ```
553: 
554: An audio segment can have one tone effect and one scene audio effect at the same time. `ToneEffectType` provides 11 tones with adjustable parameters. Voice conversion effects that require AI processing are not supported. Some resources require a CapCut subscription; refer to the application for availability.
555: 
556: #### Add Segment Filters
557: 
558: Filters are added similarly via `VideoSegment.add_filter()`. Filters support a single “intensity” parameter.
559: 
560: ```python
561: from pycapcut import FilterType
562: 
563: video_segment1.add_filter(FilterType.冷蓝, 10)  # Set intensity of "冷蓝" to 10
564: video_segment2.add_filter(FilterType.冷蓝, 50)  # Set intensity of "冷蓝" to 50
565: ```
566: 
567: #### Set Segment Blend Mode
568: 
569: Use `VideoSegment.set_mix_mode()` to set the blend mode of an overlapping video segment. `MixModeType` provides ten modes: Multiply (正片叠底), Color Dodge (颜色减淡), Color Burn (颜色加深), Linear Burn (线性加深), Soft Light (柔光), Hard Light (强光), Screen (滤色), Overlay (叠加), Lighten (变亮), and Darken (变暗). Start the lower segment at 0 seconds on the main track, and place the upper segment on a higher track:
570: 
571: ```python
572: import pycapcut as cc
573: 
574: # Assume script already exists and both video files are at least 5 seconds long
575: script.add_track(cc.TrackType.video, "Background", relative_index=0)
576: script.add_track(cc.TrackType.video, "Foreground", relative_index=2)
577: script.add_segment(cc.VideoSegment("background.mp4", cc.trange_seconds(0, duration=5)), "Background")
578: 
579: foreground = cc.VideoSegment("foreground.mp4", cc.trange_seconds(0, duration=5))
580: foreground.set_mix_mode(cc.MixModeType.正片叠底)
581: script.add_segment(foreground, "Foreground")
582: ```
583: 
584: Each segment keeps one blend mode. Repeated calls replace it with the last setting. The upper segment must overlap the lower image for the effect to be visible.
585: 
586: #### Add Chroma Keying
587: 
588: Call `VideoSegment.add_chroma()` with a `#RRGGBBAA` color. The four numeric parameters range from 0 to 100 and correspond to intensity, shadow, edge smoothing, and spill removal. Their defaults are 20, 0, 0 and 0. Call it once per segment, before adding the segment to the script. Some controls require a CapCut subscription; refer to the application for availability.
589: 
590: ```python
591: import pycapcut as cc
592: 
593: script.add_track(cc.TrackType.video, "Background", relative_index=0)
594: script.add_track(cc.TrackType.video, "Foreground", relative_index=2)
595: script.add_segment(cc.VideoSegment("background.mp4", cc.trange_seconds(0, duration=4)), "Background")
596: 
597: foreground = cc.VideoSegment("green_screen.mp4", cc.trange_seconds(1, duration=2))
598: foreground.add_chroma("#00FE00FF", intensity=36, shadow=10, edge_smooth=3, spill=26)
599: script.add_segment(foreground, "Foreground")
600: ```
601: 
602: #### Effect and Filter Tracks
603: 
604: Besides attaching effects and filters to video segments, you can create standalone effect and filter tracks and add effect/filter segments to them.
605: 
606: First, create an effect track or filter track via `ScriptFile.add_track()`. For ordering, see [Multi-Track Operations](#multi-track-operations)
607: ```python
608: script.add_track(cc.TrackType.effect, "my_effect")  # Create an effect track named "my_effect"
609: script.add_track(cc.TrackType.filter, "my_filter")  # Create a filter track named "my_filter"
610: ```
611: 
612: Then use `add_effect` and `add_filter` to add segments to those tracks:
613: ```python
614: from pycapcut import VideoSceneEffectType, FilterType, trange, trange_seconds
615: 
616: # Add a "胶片闪切" effect on the effect track, lasting 5s, with parameters
617: script.add_effect(VideoSceneEffectType.胶片闪切, trange_seconds(0, duration=5),
618:                   track_name="my_effect",  # Can be omitted if only one effect track
619:                   params=[50, None, 80])   # Set speed=50, keep intensity default (100), set texture=80
620: 
621: # Add a "冷蓝" filter to last for the entire video, intensity 70
622: # script.duration is in microseconds; use trange directly
623: script.add_filter(FilterType.冷蓝, trange(0, script.duration),
624:                   track_name="my_filter",  # Can be omitted if only one filter track
625:                   intensity=70)
626: ```
627: 
628: #### Add Segment Animations
629: 
630: Use `segment.add_animation()` to add animations. Text intro and outro animations use the effect’s default duration when omitted; pass a duration as the second argument to override it. Loop animations fill the remaining part of the text segment. To add multiple animations, call the method multiple times on the same segment.
631: 
632: > ℹ For text segments, if you need both loop and in/out animations, add in/out animations first, then the loop animation
633: 
634: Example of adding three animations to a text segment:
635: ```python
636: from pycapcut import TextIntro, TextOutro, TextLoopAnim
637: 
638: text_seg.add_animation(TextIntro.复古打字机).add_animation(TextOutro.弹簧)
639: text_seg.add_animation(TextLoopAnim.色差故障)  # Note: loop animations must be added after in/out animations
640: ```
641: 
642: 
643: ### Text and Subtitles
644: 
645: #### Add Text
646: 
647: Adding text is similar to adding video/audio segments: create a `TextSegment` and add it via `add_segment`. Font, text style, and image adjustments are specified via `font`, `style`, and `clip_settings`.
648: 
649: Example:
650: ```python
651: import pycapcut as cc
652: from pycapcut import FontType, TextStyle, ClipSettings, trange_seconds
653: 
654: # A light-blue subtitle-like text with underline and positioned like subtitles
655: seg1 = cc.TextSegment("Subtitle", trange_seconds(0, duration=10),
656:                           font=FontType.思源粗宋,
657:                           style=TextStyle(size=5.0, color=(0.7, 0.7, 1.0), underline=True, align=1),
658:                           clip_settings=ClipSettings(transform_y=-0.8))
659: ```
660: 
661: See `TextStyle` and `ClipSettings` constructors for details.
662: 
663: #### Automatic Line Wrapping
664: 
665: Text segments support auto-wrapping via `TextStyle.auto_wrapping` and `TextStyle.max_line_width`:
666: 
667: ```python
668: # Enable auto wrapping, with max line width at 70% of screen width
669: seg2 = cc.TextSegment("This is a long text; when it exceeds the set max line width, it wraps automatically.",
670:                           trange_seconds(0, duration=10),
671:                           font=FontType.思源粗宋,
672:                           style=TextStyle(size=5.0,
673:                                           auto_wrapping=True,      # Enable auto wrapping
674:                                           max_line_width=0.7))     # Max line width at 70% of screen
675: ```
676: 
677: #### Import Subtitles
678: 
679: > ℹ Currently only SRT format is supported
680: 
681: Importing subtitles essentially creates a series of texts based on each subtitle’s timestamps and content, and adds them to a track. This is done via `ScriptFile.import_srt`. Imported subtitles enable auto-wrapping by default.
682: 
683: Example:
684: ```python
685: import pycapcut as cc
686: 
687: # Assume we already have a draft object `script` (see “Quick Start”)
688: # Import subtitles into a track named "subtitle". If the track does not exist, it will be created automatically.
689: # If `style` and `clip_settings` are not specified, defaults mimic CapCut’s imported subtitle style.
690: script.import_srt("subtitle.srt", track_name="subtitle", time_offset="1.5s")  # Shift the subtitles by 1.5s
691: ```
692: 
693: The following examples are alternatives. Choose the one you need to avoid importing overlapping subtitles into the same track.
694: 
695: ```python
696: # Adjust subtitle styles using `text_style` and `clip_settings` (same semantics as in `TextSegment()`)
697: script.import_srt("subtitle.srt", track_name="subtitle",
698:                   text_style=cc.TextStyle(size=10.0, color=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)),
699:                   clip_settings=cc.ClipSettings(transform_y=0.8))  # Place subtitles at the top of the screen
700: ```
701: 
702: ```python
703: # For more complex styles or to apply animations, pass a `TextSegment` as `style_reference` (text and duration are ignored)
704: # Note animation timing does not adapt to segment length; very short subtitle segments may look odd
705: script.import_srt("subtitle.srt", track_name="subtitle", style_reference=seg1)  # Use `seg1` from “Add Text” as reference
706: ```
707: 
708: ```python
709: # By default `clip_settings` from `style_reference` is not applied. Pass `clip_settings=None` if you want to adopt it.
710: script.import_srt("subtitle.srt", track_name="subtitle", style_reference=seg1, clip_settings=None)  # Equivalent to clip_settings=seg1.clip_settings
711: ```

144:         template_path = os.path.join(self.folder_path, template_name)

150:             "speeds": [spd.export_json() for spd in self.speeds],
151:             "stickers": self.stickers,
152:             "tail_leaders": [],
153:             "text_templates": [],
154:             "texts": self.texts,
155:             "time_marks": [],
156:             "transitions": [transition.export_json() for transition in self.transitions],
157:             "video_effects": [effect.export_json() for effect in self.video_effects],
158:             "video_trackings": [],
159:             "videos": [video.export_json() for video in self.videos],

161:             "vocal_separations": []
